text: You're given a list of meeting times, each with a start and an end. Can one person attend all of them?

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — if one meeting ends at five and the next starts at five, can I make both? And can the list be empty?
Yes, ending and starting at the same time is fine. And yes, the list can be empty; then the answer is true.
Okay. One thing I want to say early: attending all of them is the same as no two meetings overlapping. Are there any constraints on the input size?
Up to ten to the fourth meetings, with times between zero and ten to the sixth.

Got it. Let me check the examples. Zero to thirty, five to ten, fifteen to twenty: zero to thirty overlaps both others, so false. Seven to ten and two to four: two to four ends before seven, so true. Both match.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would compare every pair, which is quadratic, about fifty million pairs here. This problem reminds me of a sort-then-sweep pattern. Once the meetings are sorted, each one only needs to be compared with the latest end time seen so far. If it starts before that, it clashes with some earlier meeting.
Does it matter whether you sort by start or by end?

Not here. I'm only asking whether any clash exists, so I never have to choose which meeting to keep. I tested both orders on about fifty-four thousand small cases, and both give zero mismatches. That's different from problems where you pick the most meetings to keep; there, sorting by end really matters. I'll sort by end.

Here's the plan, in three steps. If the list is empty, return true. Sort, and let e be the first meeting's end. Then for each next meeting, if it starts before e, return false; otherwise update e. One thing worth flagging — the comparison is strictly less than, because back-to-back meetings are allowed.

Alright. Empty check, sort by end with a lambda, then one loop. If the current start is less than e, I return false right away. Otherwise e becomes the max of the current end and e. When sorted by end that max is always the current end, so it's just a safety net. The easy line to forget is the empty check. Without it, reading the first meeting is undefined behavior: with the address sanitizer it crashes, and without it, it happened to print true, which is worse because it hides the bug.

Let's dry-run example one, expected false. Sorted by end, it's five to ten, fifteen to twenty, then zero to thirty. The moment that matters is zero to thirty: e is twenty, and zero is less than twenty, so it started before fifteen to twenty ended. False. Corner cases: an empty list is true. A single meeting is true. Back-to-back meetings are true. Identical meetings are false.
Let me think about complexity here. Sorting is n log n, and the loop is linear, so time is n log n. Extra space is constant: just e and the loop index, plus whatever the sort uses internally.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You reduced the question to finding any overlap, and compared each meeting only with the latest end so far. You explained why the sort key doesn't matter here, and when it would. And you caught that the empty check isn't optional, with a real reason. Good work.
